title: A NaN check written as == Float.NaN never fires, and fcmpl quietly becomes fcmpg
summary: The interpreter's `fcmp` implements `fcmpg` and `fcmpl` with four branches: less, greater, equal, and the unordered case that the two opcodes decide differently. A developer moves the unordered case to the front, written as `a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN`, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison. The regression proof against the previous version finds an input with a NaN on which `fcmpl` now pushes 1 instead of -1: a comparison with `Float.NaN` is false for every operand, including NaN.

change.description: Handle the unordered case first, with an explicit test for NaN, and write the rest as `a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0`. The old code reached the NaN case by falling through three failed comparisons, which read as an accident; the new code names it. The tests for ordering, -0.0, the infinities and NaN under `fcmpg` all pass.

risk: The two opcodes exist so that javac can compile `a < b` as `fcmpg` and `a > b` as `fcmpl`, each sending a NaN down the false branch; with `fcmpl` answering 1 for a NaN, a guest program's `if (x > y)` with `x` NaN takes the true branch, and `x > y && x < y` can hold at once. Nothing crashes: a sort of floats with a NaN in it comes out in the wrong order, a `Math.max` written by hand returns the wrong operand, a bounds check lets a NaN through. The test with a NaN exercises `fcmpg`, for which the broken check and the fall-through agree; `fcmpl` with a NaN is untested, and `x == Float.NaN` is the comparison Java programmers are warned about in the first chapter on floating point, which is exactly why a reviewer who sees it in a line that says "NaN" in its comment reads past it.
explanation: The regression proof compiles both versions of `fcmp` into one program and asks JBMC for an input on which they differ. Floats are bit-vectors to the solver, NaN among them, and it finds one in the first stage: a NaN operand with the `fcmpl` rule, on which the old code returns -1 and the new code 1, because `a == Float.NaN` is false even when `a` is NaN and the three-way comparison that follows has no case for an unordered pair. The tool replays the input in its interpreter and shows both outcomes. The point of the proof is that it covers every float, NaN and the signed zeros included, where a test covers the values its author thought of.
resolution: Revert, or write the check as `Float.isNaN(a) || Float.isNaN(b)` (which is `a != a`), and add the `fcmpl` NaN test the regression proof shows was missing. Better: keep the fall-through form, with a comment that the fourth branch is the unordered case, since it is the form in which the specification states the instruction.
provenance: Constructed from JVMS §6.5 (`fcmpg` and `fcmpl`) and the classic `x == Float.NaN` mistake.

references.title: JVMS §6.5, fcmpg and fcmpl: the two instructions differ only in their treatment of NaN
JLS §15.21.1, Numerical Equality Operators: a comparison with NaN is false
